analysis.one_liner: Replaces private health insurance with a single government program covering every U.S. resident, with no copays or deductibles.
analysis.headline: The Medicare for All bill drew 65 House Democrats as sponsors and cosponsors, but was sent to three committees and never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put every person living in the United States into one government-run health program — an expanded Medicare — covering all medically necessary care, including doctor visits, hospital care, prescriptions, dental, vision, hearing, mental health, and long-term care, with no premiums, deductibles, or copays. It would be paid for with existing federal health dollars plus new taxes on the top 5% of earners, payroll and self-employment income, unearned income, and stock and bond trades. Private insurers could no longer sell plans that duplicate the public benefit, and investor-owned hospitals would have to convert to nonprofit status, with owners compensated. The bill was introduced in February 2013, referred to three House committees, and died without any hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident, especially the uninsured and the tens of millions who have coverage but can't afford to use it: the bill gives everyone a card entitling them to all medically necessary care — including dental, vision, hearing aids, long-term care, and mental health — with no deductibles, copays, or coinsurance. Patients would keep free choice of doctor and hospital. People with jobs tied to employer insurance would no longer face losing coverage when they change or lose jobs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially the uninsured and underinsured

how_it_helps.text: All individuals residing in the United States would be covered, receive a card in the mail, and be presumed eligible when they show up for care, with a two-page application.

Covered benefits include all medically necessary services — primary and preventive care, inpatient and outpatient care, emergency care, prescription drugs, long-term care, mental health, full dental services, vision care, hearing aids, and substance abuse treatment — with no deductibles, copayments, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing.

The program would be funded by existing federal health revenues, higher income taxes on the top 5% of earners, a progressive payroll tax, a tax on unearned income, and a small tax on stock and bond transactions, while federal spending on Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP would be transferred into the new program.

Clerical, administrative, and billing workers whose jobs are eliminated would get first priority in retraining and job placement plus two years of salary-parity transition benefits, up to $100,000 a year.
The program would negotiate prescription drug prices, run a formulary promoting generics, and use bulk procurement to lower drug costs.

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers, whose core business of duplicating the public benefit would become unlawful; the top 5% of income earners, who would pay higher income taxes; all workers and self-employed people through a progressive payroll tax; investors, through a new tax on unearned income and on stock and bond trades; and owners of for-profit hospitals and clinics, who would be required to convert to nonprofit status (compensated for losses over 15 years through Treasury bonds). Insurance-company billing staff would lose jobs, though with retraining and transition pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private insurers, top earners, investors, for-profit providers

drawbacks.text: Private health insurers would be barred from selling any coverage duplicating the program's benefits, meaning the roughly employer-based and individual-market plans most Americans had at the time would be replaced rather than kept as an option.

The bill raises taxes at the same time it eliminates premiums and out-of-pocket costs: higher income taxes on the top 5% of earners, a new progressive payroll and self-employment tax, a tax on unearned income, and a tax on stock and bond transactions, so many households would pay more in taxes even as they stop paying premiums.

Investor-owned hospitals, nursing homes, and clinics could not participate unless they converted to not-for-profit status, ending for-profit ownership in the provider industry even though owners would be compensated for losses through Treasury bond payments over 15 years.

Tens of thousands of billing, clerical, and insurance-administration jobs would be eliminated, and while the bill provides two years of salary-parity transition benefits capped at $100,000 a year, it does not guarantee comparable work afterward.

The bill's funding sources are stated as categories, not set rates, and the bill received no congressional cost estimate, so whether the new taxes would fully cover the program's costs — and whether global budgets would restrain hospital spending or produce rationing pressure — was never tested or scored.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real and substantial: everyone in the country would get comprehensive coverage with zero cost at the point of care, financed by taxes concentrated on high earners, investors, and the elimination of a large private insurance bureaucracy. An honest supporter would acknowledge three serious costs: the forced disappearance of private plans most Americans had, real job losses in insurance administration (partially cushioned by the transition fund), and a funding structure that was never independently costed. The design also concentrates payment-rate-setting power in a government director, which supporters view as cost control and critics view as government rationing risk. On balance the bill's benefits are broad and its costs are concentrated and transition-related — but none of this was ever tested in committee or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and split among three House committees, and none of them ever held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on February 13, 2013, joined by 64 Democratic cosponsors; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it.
The Speaker referred the bill to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Natural Resources Committees, and it was then referred to subcommittees in mid-February 2013.

No hearing, markup, or committee vote appears in the bill's action history after the initial referrals, and the bill received no floor action for the remainder of the 113th Congress, which ended January 3, 2015.

The CRS summary confirms the bill would have established a single public program covering all U.S. residents, banned duplicating private insurance, and funded the program with taxes on top earners, payroll, unearned income, and financial transactions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, for-profit hospital owners, and other concentrated health-industry interests kept the existing system in place, because the bill was never allowed to reach a hearing or vote; ordinary Americans' coverage stayed exactly as it was.

sides.party_line_note: All 65 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill went to committees chaired by Republicans and never moved again; no Republican supported it.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful for private insurers to sell coverage duplicating the public program, ending their core business model; they could sell only extras like cosmetic surgery coverage. Insurers had nothing to gain from the bill and the existing system's continuation is their gain.

Investor-owned institutions could not participate in the program unless they converted to not-for-profit status, though owners would be compensated for financial losses via Treasury bond payments spread over 15 years. For ordinary people this removes investor return as a driver of health costs but also removes an ownership option.

The program would negotiate drug prices annually, use bulk procurement, and run a formulary favoring generics, cutting industry pricing power — while universal coverage would guarantee drug demand and patient volume. The industry's interest in preserving its current pricing runs against patients' interest in lower drug costs.

industries.industry: Insurance billing and health administration workers
industries.note: Jobs eliminated by reduced paperwork would be cut, but the bill gives these workers first priority in retraining and two years of salary-parity transition benefits up to $100,000 a year, so most would face a hard transition rather than an open-ended loss.
A small tax on stock and bond transactions plus a tax on unearned income would directly raise trading and investment costs, a burden concentrated on high-income investors and financial firms.

industries.industry: Nonprofit hospitals, clinics, and nonprofit HMOs
industries.note: Public or nonprofit institutions would receive global budgets or capitation payments as participating providers, putting them on a stable funded footing inside the program. Nonprofit HMOs that deliver care in their own facilities with salaried clinicians could keep participating.
